summary: A white paper from INFN stressing the key points to consider for an IPng plan. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A physics research group lists what matters most to them for the next Internet.

subtitle: A research network's priorities: solve address space and routing in parallel, not separately.

tldr.problem: The IPng effort could fragment into separate initiatives for address exhaustion, routing efficiency, and flat address space instead of solving all three together.
tldr.mechanism: Design IPng to address space, hierarchical routing, and policy-based routing as an integrated whole, informed by real DECnet-to-CLNS migration experience.
tldr.outcome: A unified solution that scales, allows flexible administration, and lets sites transition at their own pace while maintaining IPv4 connectivity.

today: RFC 1676 is Informational from August 1994. IPv6 eventually adopted hierarchical addressing and policy-based routing as INFN recommended, though it did not choose CLNS. The IPv4-to-IPv6 transition remains ongoing in 2026, decades later—validating INFN's warning that without firm deadline discipline, coexistence becomes indefinite.

sections.title: INFN's View of IPng Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 1676 comes from INFN (Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare), the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics, through its network team. The authors—Ghiselli, Salomoni and Vistoli—represent a nationwide research network providing access to high-energy physics laboratories and facilitating researcher communications.

They submit their experience and ideas from operating this specialized, demanding network. They emphasize that IPng planning should solve address exhaustion, routing efficiency, and the flat address space problem as one integrated challenge, not as separate initiatives.
sections.eli5: INFN is a physics research network that has dealt with network transitions before. They want IPng to tackle all the hard problems together.

sections.title: General Requirements and Network Layer Design
sections.content:
INFN's general requirements emphasize transparency to end-user applications (applications should not know about the transition) and flexibility to accommodate new communication technologies and topology changes. At the network layer, INFN recommends that IPng continue to provide datagram service like IP does. They note that CLNS (the OSI Connectionless Network Service) could be an ideal foundation: it has been proven in production, uses 20-byte NSAP addresses (sufficient for future growth), and supports hierarchical addressing for flexible administrative delegation and policy-based routing.

Hierarchical address formats can organize administration and management in ways that satisfy both delegated responsibility and routing performance, solving the flat address space problem that limits IPv4.
sections.eli5: Applications should work without knowing the network changed. The network layer should use 20-byte addresses with hierarchical structure so organizations can each manage their own sections.

sections.title: Routing and Transition Strategy
sections.content:
INFN does not consider the routing protocol choice fundamental; routing protocols can be improved or changed without affecting end systems. However, NSAP aggregation, hierarchical topology and hierarchical routing algorithms are key. Policy-based routing is essential for the complex, growing IPv4 network topology. INFN also advocates multicast support and warns against source routing, which complicates software and contradicts connectionless philosophy.

For transition, INFN favors a dual-stack approach over translation mechanisms, based on experience migrating DECnet to DECnet/OSI. Dual stack is simpler to develop and deploy at different rates across organizations. However, it is important to set a deadline for backward compatibility to avoid perpetual maintenance of both stacks; pure IPng with global connectivity should become the goal once there are no IPv4-only hosts.
sections.eli5: Routing protocols can change anytime, but address hierarchy and policy-based routing matter a lot. Let each organization switch when ready, but set an end date for running both old and new together.

sections.title: Lessons from DECnet Migration
sections.content:
INFN's experience with the DECnet to DECnet/OSI transition informs all its recommendations. Administrative and network management aspects matter as much as protocol design. Organizations need tools, examples and the freedom to transition at their own pace. However, perpetual dual-stack operation creates problems: address space constraints continue, both routing suites must be supported, and tunneling solutions for IPv4 islands give poor performance.

INFN recommends maintaining IPv4 connectivity and dual-stack support on end systems for a defined timeframe, then retiring it. Without such discipline, the transition will never complete.
sections.eli5: Switching networks is not just a technical problem; it is an organizational one. Set clear timelines or the old network will never really go away.

references.text: Gross, P. (ed.), "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
